effect_estimate.comment: In pooled two-way FE DID models (Table 2, N = 219 observations; 19 treated and 54 PSM control census tracks), ZEIS implementation increased sewage access via public network by 22.161 percentage points (SE = 10.254, p < 0.05) and piped water access via public network by 9.107 percentage points (SE = 5.073, p < 0.10) without district linear trends (Panel A), and increased sewage access by 18.970 percentage points (SE = 9.187, p < 0.05) and water access by 8.086 percentage points (SE = 6.336, not significant) with district linear trends (Panel B). In dynamic DID models for tracts treated in 1993-1996 with district linear trends (Table 3, N = 216 observations; 18 treated and 54 PSM control census tracks), medium-run (2000; 4-7 years exposure) effects were +15.471 percentage points (SE = 7.292, p < 0.05) for public-network sewage access and +2.178 percentage points (SE = 6.323, NS) for public-network water access; long-run (2010; 14-17 years exposure) effects were +23.479 percentage points (SE = 12.189, p < 0.10) for public-network sewage access, +15.702 percentage points (SE = 7.105, p < 0.05) for public-network water access, +11.962 percentage points (SE = 4.362, p < 0.05) for homeownership, and -0.133 (SE = 0.263, NS) for mean bathrooms per household. Results remained robust when using 84 non-treated slum tracts as controls (Table 4: 2010 water +15.524 pp, p < 0.05; sewage +24.511 pp, p < 0.10), excluding neighboring control tracts (Table 5: 2010 water +16.877 pp, p < 0.05; sewage +28.612 pp, p < 0.05), and controlling for log mean household income (Table 6: 2010 water +15.354 pp, p < 0.05; sewage +23.815 pp, p < 0.10).
effect_estimate.value: Pooled DID with district trends (N = 219 census-track-year observations): public-network sewage access +18.970 percentage points (SE = 9.187, p < 0.05), public-network water access +8.086 percentage points (SE = 6.336, NS; +9.107 pp, SE = 5.073, p < 0.10 without district trends). Dynamic DID with district trends for 1993-1996 cohort (N = 216 observations): in 2000 (4-7 years exposure), sewage network access +15.471 percentage points (SE = 7.292, p < 0.05) and water network access +2.178 percentage points (SE = 6.323, NS); in 2010 (14-17 years exposure), sewage network access +23.479 percentage points (SE = 12.189, p < 0.10), water network access +15.702 percentage points (SE = 7.105, p < 0.05), homeownership +11.962 percentage points (SE = 4.362, p < 0.05), and bathrooms per household -0.133 (SE = 0.263, NS).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Quasi-experimental PSM + two-way fixed-effects DID panel evaluation (appraised with ROBINS-I at Moderate overall risk of bias) estimating the causal effect of municipal ZEIS zoning and regularization legislation on public water and sewage network coverage, supported by baseline covariate balance, census-tract and year fixed effects, district linear trends, neighbourhood-clustered standard errors, and robustness checks across unmatched slum controls, ZEIS share cutoffs (50%-100%), spatial-spillover exclusions, and income controls. Caveats noted by the authors include a single pre-intervention wave (1991) preventing pre-trend event-study testing and aggregate census-tract observations rather than household-level panels.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS) and the PREZEIS regularization framework—municipal land-use zoning and urban planning instruments demarcating eligible low-income settlements, applying differentiated building and urbanistic parameters (accommodation of informal settlement morphology), and promoting land tenure and property regularization (via adverse possession/usucapião on private land and Granting of the Right to Use/Concessão de Direito Real de Uso on public land, plus restrictions on lot subdivision/reunification).

sample_size.comment: Citywide universe of 962 temporally compatible census tracks in Recife observed across three Demographic Census waves (1991, 2000, and 2010; originally 962, 1,212, and 1,854 census tracks respectively), comprising 513 tracts with ZEIS presence by 2010 (132 newly treated in 1991-2010 and 381 treated pre-1991) and 449 never-treated tracts. Primary pooled DID sample (Table 2): 73 census tracks (19 treated tracts with >90% ZEIS territory and 54 PSM control tracts), yielding 219 census-track-year observations. Dynamic DID sample for 1993-1996 cohort (Tables 3 and 6): 72 census tracks (18 treated and 54 PSM control tracts), yielding 216 observations. Robustness samples: 102 census tracks / 306 observations using 84 non-treated slum tracts as controls (Table 4), and 56-57 census tracks (18-19 treated, 38 control) / 168 observations excluding neighboring non-treated tracts (Table 5).

study_design.comment: Quasi-experimental panel evaluation combining Propensity Score Matching (nearest-neighbor logit matching on 1991 baseline covariates) with two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID) regressions (including census-tract fixed effects, census-year fixed effects, district-specific linear trends, and neighborhood-clustered standard errors) across three decennial census waves (1991 pre-intervention; 2000 and 2010 post-intervention).
